book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only
samples: Robert Arp's introduction explains that Homeland's jihadist material (Nazir, Hamid, Brody, 9/11) drew him in and previews the book's philosophizing with a sample argument: whether morality needs God. He argues jihadists ground ethics in Allah's commands, but since faith defies rational proof, competing conceptions of God conflict, and scripture (Abraham and Isaac, the Flood, the Egyptian firstborn, the genocide commands in 1 Samuel and Hosea) has God commanding atrocities, either the terrorists' God is evil or morality is better grounded in reason without God. The dilemma he poses - a good God would not command 9/11, so the command conception or God's goodness must go - is the Euthyphro structure applied to terrorism.

Jason Iuliano asks whether the Brody who lied to Helen Walker about Tom Walker's death is the same person as the one who beat Walker, and whether 2011 Brody is responsible for 2003 Brody's acts. He contrasts the biological criterion (same human animal), the psychological criterion of overlapping memories and intentions (so Brody remembering his family remains the same person), and the narrative identity theory Carrie invokes in 'Q&A' when she says Nazir pulled Brody apart and put him back together as someone else. A Carrie thought experiment about ECT outcomes and a Nazir mind-swap of Brody's and Walker's psychologies argue that only narrative coherence captures whom we should praise, blame, and anticipate surviving.

Talia Morag reads Brody's colliding roles - Marine, congressman, father, Muslim, follower of Abu Nazir - and Carrie's unstable ones (CIA agent, bipolar patient, lover) through Korsgaard's notion of practical identities, whose contradictory obligations (kill and not kill) demand reconciliation. Following Kierkegaard's advice to rethink labels like 'Christian', Brody reinterprets his suicide tape as acting 'as a Marine' against domestic enemies - a rationalizing move the chapter treats as bordering on bad faith - while Dana's phone call in 'Marine One' reasserts the father identity and stops the bombing. Carrie's 'Q&A' re-description of Brody as a good man and future hero shows identities are constructed through choices, Sartre's point that we are not summaries of our past.

Laszlo Kajtar uses Brody's Complex PTSD - torture, forced killing of Walker, intrusive nightmares attacking Jessica - to test theories of personal identity. Animalism says Brody is the same biological organism before and after captivity, while the psychological approach, sourced in Locke's memory criterion, traces continuity of beliefs, desires, and intentions and finds it disrupted by trauma and Nazir's brainwashing, which filled the hole trauma left after Issa's death. Kajtar argues both miss the first-personal 'sense of self': like many PTSD sufferers, Brody feels he is not the person he was, and 'It's like she doesn't know who I actually am now' shows identity shattered from the inside.

John Karavitis evaluates four suicide events: Afsal Hamid's suicide in CIA custody, Aileen Morgan's cutting her throat with a lens, Brody's aborted suicide bombing, and Carrie's ECT as a 'suicide' of her old self. Kant's absolute ban on suicide (it denies your humanity) clashes with Seneca's Stoic counsel that a life of miserable captivity need not be continued, and with Singer's utilitarian permission of euthanasia that reduces suffering - under both, Hamid's and Aileen's suicides are defensible while Brody's emotionally driven bombing is not. Dana's plea that her father is needed recasts Aristotle's point that suicide wrongs the community, and Sloterdijk's analysis of rage turned on oneself frames Carrie's amoral self-destruction.

Brittany Lorenz and Adam Barkman apply the Greek four-loves framework (storge, eros, philia, agape) to Homeland's relationships. Terrorism breaks storge by destroying comfort in familiar places; broken eros appears in the Brody-Jessica-Mike-Carrie square and Mira's lover who loves 'making love' rather than her; philia falters because Brody hides his Islam from Jessica, and Abu Nazir's bond with Brody is Aristotle's friendship of utility, dissolving when the advantage ceases. Brody's agape for country is broken because fighting abroad violates his prior duties as husband and father, so the show offers only glimpses of loves that might be redeemed.

book: 086 - Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything
samples: The editors' introduction argues that Girls is philosophical because it is stark, raw, and accurate about what is common to human existence: identity, friendship, expectations, and ultimately the meaning of life. It claims Hannah, for all her horribleness (the funeral pitch to her dying editor's widow, doing coke to write truthfully about drugs), follows Socrates's call to know thyself in a millennial register. It then surveys the volume's approaches - existentialism, business ethics, the seven deadly sins, Daoism and Confucianism, Freud, Kristeva - as ways of knowing Hannah, Marnie, Jessa, Shosh, Ray, and Adam, and thereby ourselves.

Frost argues that critics who call Girls unwatchable because Hannah steals the hotel housekeeper's tip and the characters are unlikeable are watching television the wrong way. Using Adorno's 'How to Look at Television,' he shows how mainstream standardized shows (Friends and its copies) pre-digest viewing, how Sex and the City exemplifies Adorno's ideological 'fake-realism,' and how hidden messages of adjustment work through audience identification - none of which Girls permits with its raw sex scenes, Hannah's unglamorous body, and Jessa's non-judged promiscuity. Because identification with Hannah, Marnie, and Jessa (the diary-reading, the request to Laird for heroin) is impossible, Girls escapes the culture industry and exercises the viewer's critical faculties toward the Kantian autonomy and emancipation Adorno demands - which is also why role-model feminist criticism (Catherine Scott's) misses the point.

Robison-Greene defends Girls against the twin criticisms that it is bad feminism (Hannah 'sluttin' around' jokes, Adam's degrading sex with Hannah) and irresponsibly all-white. She argues there is no single correct conception of feminism from which to judge Dunham, that 'demeaning sex is anti-feminist, so portraying it is anti-feminist' is an invalid argument (by analogy with portraying racism in 12 Years a Slave), and notes MacKinnon's dominance view that sex itself may be inherently demeaning only to conclude the debate is legitimate, not settled against the show. On race, she contends Dunham writing authentically from her own half-Jew, half-WASP experience produces better art than tokenism would, and that the obligation to fix representation falls on networks and creators with the relevant experience, not on punishing one writer.

McCrossin asks whether Adam's Season Two finale run across Brooklyn to break down the door of a dangerously unraveling Hannah ('I was always here') is heroic, set against Hannah's 'You don't need to be like a hero' chair-and-mattress scene and Adam's 'I don't want to help... I was doing it because I love you' quarrel. He argues an act is heroic - being an 'Extraordinary Samaritan' like Wesley Autrey, the Subway Samaritan, unlike the trained Sullenberger - only when done on purpose to help, not from obligation, training, or love's compulsion, testing the point with Batman's motives. Since Adam insists no one ever does anything from a want to help, his rescue's heroic status is left genuinely open.

Greene constructs the conditions of a 'legitimate spoiler' - the thing cannot be too old (with never-expiring exceptions like Darth Vader being Luke's father, Snape killing Dumbledore, and the Planet of the Apes reveal), cannot be common knowledge (Anne Boleyn's beheading, the Titanic hitting the iceberg), and must be significant rather than mundane. Applying them, he concludes Girls cannot be conventionally spoiled: nobody 'ships' Hannah and Adam the way audiences shipped Ross and Rachel, because the show's plot turns are mere backdrop for its conversations and meltdowns. The only true way to spoil Girls is to reveal its hilariously written lines in advance.

Blessing and Wezowiczi test theories of life's meaning on the two narcissists of Girls: Hannah, whose purpose-driven pursuit of being a writer (manufacturing experiences, ignoring her father's medical procedure) shows that goal achievement alone collapses into Taylor's and Camus's Sisyphus problem, and Jessa, whose 'life addict' desire-satisfaction illustrates the Nietzschean live-in-the-moment view the authors find reckless and irresponsible. Using Wielenberg's excrement-eater and the subjectivist/objectivist debate, they land on Susan Wolf's 'loving objects that are worthy of love,' then argue via Socrates's examined life and Sartre's bad faith that neither Hannah's phony narrative nor Jessa's protective persona counts as authentic, examined living.

book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
samples: The editor's introduction argues that Adventure Time is philosophy in disguise: its theme-song promise of 'very distant lands' describes the philosopher's trek into unpopular, even hated ideas, and the show treats 'crazy' questions as fun rather than frightening. It names the questions the book will chase—whether Finn was fated to lose his arm, whether the Ice King is really a bad guy, what evil really means—and claims that since common sense has always turned out to be wrong (matter isn't solid, the Earth moves), the childlike willingness to reconsider everything is a philosophical virtue. Philosophy, like the show, is an adventure best taken with a friend.

Karavitis argues Finn's 'Finn-losophy' is a metaphysics that prefers magic over Princess Bubblegum's science, and that this choice shapes his ethics: magic is the 'easy way out' requiring no understanding (Jake's stretching, the Glasses of Nerdicon), while science demands observation, experiment, and falsifiable ideas—'reality is the ultimate spell-checker.' Because magic promises instant gratification, Finn rushes into danger ('Wizard,' 'Donny,' the Goblin Kingdom) behind an inflexible hero code, and his altruism misfires, as the never-ending prize-winning battles of the 'Mystery Train' episode illustrate. The chapter concludes that your view of how the world works—magical or scientific—determines whether you can grow ethically at all.

Leonard reads Ooo through Heidegger's contrast between technological and poetic frames of mind: Princess Bubblegum's BGCCTV, Goliad, and the James clone mission treat candy people as manipulable stock, while the Lich is technological thinking perfected—pure efficiency aimed at 'the extinction of all life'—and Finn is the poet who values things for what they are, risks Heidegger's 'venture,' and battles Death in 'Death in Bloom' as if in a concert. On Heidegger's definition of art as 'the setting-itself-into-work of truth,' Marceline's songs and Jake's imagined lava show creation disclosing reality. Magic, spread by the Mushroom War, sits between the two modes, and only Finn's poetic exuberance can check Bubblegum's slide toward order at any cost.

Caballeros argues that political legitimacy in Ooo runs through parenthood: Princess Bubblegum rules the citizens she created ('You made me... you are my Glob'), the Ice King is redeemed when we learn Simon protected child Marceline, and the Flame King and Hunson Abadeer forfeit standing as fathers. Using Hobbes's view that a ruler is legitimate insofar as he protects his subjects, the chapter asks whether Bubblegum's protection-cum-manipulation—sabotaging Finn to let James die, jailing Tree Trunks—still counts, and it contrasts justified rebellion (Flame Princess deposing her father, Marceline resisting Abadeer) with Lumpy Space Princess's disastrous one. Good parenting, like good government, earns obedience; bad parenting loses the crown.

Gale and Barkman treat post-Mushroom-War Ooo as a state-of-nature laboratory for liberalism's three founders. The Forest Wizard who cages Finn in 'Storytelling' is Hobbes's Leviathan, kept in power by fear yet moderated by self-interest (Goblin King Xergiok's fall shows the leash); Princess Bubblegum's Candy Kingdom is Locke's civil society where citizens trade private revenge for impartial law—her lawful bow to Lemongrab shows she rules by contract, not fear; and 'City of Thieves' illustrates Rousseau's claim that property corrupts natural goodness, with Finn and Jake as his uncorrupted natural people. The chapter concludes that the rights language these thinkers forged is what keeps both Ooo and our world from sliding back into a war of all against all.

Montoya tests Simon's choice to sacrifice his sanity by wearing the crown to save child Marceline against three ethical theories. Aquinas's doctrine of double effect clears him because the intended good (saving her life) outweighs the merely foreseen side effect (her tears, his possible future evils); Kant's categorical imperative rules out universalizing 'let children die to save myself,' since a world of universal using destroys the rule itself; and a fountain case where Finn must choose between world-saving plans and a drowning candy child separates act from rule utilitarianism, with rule utilitarianism preserving the duty to rescue. All three converge on the verdict that Simon, not Finn, is Ooo's greatest hero.

book: 088 - Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later
samples: The introduction argues that Justified grips its audience because nothing in it is black-and-white: even Mags Bennett has some good in her, even Art gives Raylan a black eye, and Harlan's crime is bred by coal-industry exploitation while religion (Billy St. Cyr's Last Chance Salvation Church, Boyd's born-again congregation of ex-cons) may be salvation or a grift. Its central example is the pilot's Miami rooftop scene, where Raylan gives hitman Tommy Bucks twenty-four hours to leave town and then kills him when the clock runs out, raising the question the whole book pursues: is Raylan justified, or is it murder dressed up as cleaning up Harlan County? It closes by previewing the book's essays in ethics, political philosophy, epistemology, metaphysics, and logic.

The chapter argues Boyd Crowder personifies coolness - composure, wily cleverness, unconventionality, intelligence, likability - as shown in the 'Cottonmouth' payroll-robbery scene where he turns his flip phone into a room bug, overhears Kyle planning to blow him up in the mine, and lets the plotters kill themselves. Jon Cotton borrows Wittgenstein's family-resemblance model to define coolness as an indefinable cluster of traits (with Dewey Crowe as the agreed uncool case), and reaches back to Socrates' defining of ethical virtues and the Republic's just, well-ordered soul to argue that coolness is a genuine ethical virtue - the excellence of a properly functioning person - in a scientific, post-religious ethics.

The chapter juxtaposes the 1992 no-knock raid in which 84-year-old paraplegic Annie Rae Dixon was shot in her bed with Raylan's pilot-episode ultimatum to Tommy Bucks, arguing both deaths count as 'justified' only because aggressive proactive policing manufactured the lethal encounter. It catalogues Raylan's tactics - provoking draws, kidnapping the cartel chief's niece and Dickie Bennett, the lucky-sniper standoff at the Bennett compound - and asks whether we want our police to be judge, jury, and executioner. On the deontological approach Raylan's routine lawbreaking cannot be justified whatever the results, and even on the consequentialist approach the war-on-drugs data (soaring murder rates in targeted neighborhoods, mass incarceration) suggest proactive policing fails on its own terms.

The chapter argues coal made Boyd Crowder possible: company scrip, Bloody Harlan's union-busting terror, black lung (Boyd's would-be assassin takes the bridge job because mining ruined his lungs), and Black Pike's mountaintop removal leave Harlan no viable work outside the mines, so crime is the rational alternative. It reads this through Hegel's 'rabble' from the Philosophy of Right - civil society is never wealthy enough to prevent an excess of poverty, and the rabble loses the honor of self-support - plus Marcuse's affluent-society critique of an existence that 'violently defends its own servitude'. Boyd's outlawry, which sets its own code above mere criminality, is a rebellion against being pushed into the rabble, and Hegel's remedy of emigration explains why leaving Harlan is the only escape, though the coal train hauls coal out while the people stay.

The chapter applies Critical Race Theory - Derrick Bell's theses that racism is ordinary and structural, advances white interests (interest convergence, illustrated by his reading of Brown v. Board), and that race is socially constructed - to argue Justified reinforces white superiority. Its Black characters are overwhelmingly criminals (bookie Arnold Pinter, enforcer Curtis Mims, bail jumper Jody Adair, drug-dealing butcher Ellstin Limehouse, who disciplines Bernard with the lye pit), law enforcement is white, and even the positive Rachel Brooks remains a bit-part mystery. Following media research on differential racialization and the cumulative effect of TV portrayals, it concludes the show is one more vehicle teaching viewers that whites keep African Americans in line.

The chapter turns Raylan's claim that shooting Tommy Bucks was 'justified' into a question of epistemic justification, expounding Plato's Meno definition of knowledge as justified true belief, Gettier's 1963 counterexamples (rebuilt with Boyd truly but luckily predicting that a marshal will be arrested), and the repairs of Goldman's no-false-causal-link condition and Harman's inference to the best explanation. It then grades the show's reasoners: Raylan knows the Crowes rather than Boyd killed Wade Messer, Boyd knows Cassie milks the revival snakes' venom, Art Mullen does not yet know Raylan helped Winona return the evidence-room money, and gut-feeling victims like Ellen May do not know what they saw. Against Humean skepticism about cause and effect it defends inductive, detective-style knowledge - Raylan can know who done it without courtroom proof.

book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different
samples: The editor's introduction ('hello.') recounts his own path from an Apple IIe through a PC interlude back to the iPod and iPhone, and frames Jobs's arc: a bold, brash entrepreneur of modest means who revolutionized computers, music, phones, and movies, yet was petulant, insensitive, and cruel, a 'barefoot billionaire hippy capitalist' shaped by Sixties counterculture and Eastern spirituality who set out to 'make a ding in the universe.' It presents the book as neither demonization nor hagiography but thoughtful, mostly philosophical examinations of Jobs's life, work, and cultural impact from many points of view.

Mahon reads Jobs's 'reality distortion field'—the phrase Apple engineer Bud Tribble borrowed from the illusion-casting Talosians of Star Trek's 'The Cage' and 'The Menagerie'—through the ethics of deception. He argues that unlike the Talosians' non-consensual illusions (trapping Captain Pike to breed slaves), Jobs mostly changed people's beliefs about what was possible rather than deceiving them, often believed his own claims (even about his cancer), and sometimes freed people from false beliefs as the 1984 'Big Brother' Macintosh ad dramatized, so the field that produced the 'insanely great' Stevenotes, the impossible Macintosh schedule, and Dilbert's Dogbert parody needed little moral justification—and made Jobs's revolutionized industries possible.

Biondi argues the 'counter-cultural capitalist' is no paradox: Jobs succeeded not as a Gordon Gekko-style greedy capitalist but through the creative individualism of the cognitive counter-culture—the garage techno-geeks—who pursued their own vision rather than the bottom line. She traces the greedy-capitalist stereotype to Glaucon's Ring-of-Gyges challenge in Plato's Republic (people act justly only from fear of punishment), Hobbes's restless desire for power after power, and Marx and Engels's picture of alienated wage slavery under capitalism, with Rawls as the toleration-only-if-redistributed alternative. Jobs's hippie exterior (drugs, fruitarianism, Zen) masked an entrepreneur who, in Rand's 'creative mind' mold, put a ding in the universe through products like the iPad instead of philanthropy.

Noel measures Jobs against the four cardinal virtues from Plato's Republic and finds him wanting: imprudent (NeXT, the Lisa), unjust (taking the GUI from Xerox PARC, 'more fun to be a pirate'), intemperate (cruel outbursts like the 'dogshit for icing' cake), with only a brash, mind-changing courage. Drawing on Aristotle's golden mean from the Nicomachean Ethics, Nietzsche's master-slave morality and his Will to Power line about the man who 'determines values' for millennia, and Joseph Campbell's hero's journey, he argues entrepreneurs are a breed apart whose real virtues are independence of mind, vision, and audacity—and that Jobs, the anti-social creator who would not fit in, changed the world precisely because the cardinal virtues were 'prison walls' to him.

Munkittrick argues that because personhood cannot be defined (trait lists like 'long-term planning' are circular) and behavior cannot prove an inner mind—as Searle's Chinese Room thought experiment shows—people have always identified persons intuitively, and Pixar trained Millennials to do exactly that. He reads the Pixar canon in three stages: Toy Story's self-aware Buzz as nascent non-human personhood, the Human-as-Partner films (Ratatouille's Remy and Linguini, WALL-E and EVE, Monsters, Inc.'s Sully and Boo, Up's Carl and Dug) as mutual recognition of persons across species lines, and The Incredibles as showing that even enhanced 'super-humans' face otherization—so a generation primed by these films will accept AI, animals, and uplifted beings as bearers of rights.

Hicks starts from young Jobs the 'little terror' expelled from third grade and asks whether he failed the school system or the system failed him, answering that America's entrepreneurs are produced by culture outside school—garage workshops, Heathkits, dirt-bike ramps, and parents who back initiative—rather than rows, rote learning, and standardized tests. He catalogues the entrepreneurial character traits Jobs displayed (informed creative judgment, ambition and integrity like the carpenter's hidden plywood, initiative calling Bill Hewlett at home, courage, perseverance through the Lisa, NeXT, and Pixar losses, win-win trade, leadership) and proposes risk-exercise curricula, Montessori methods, and programs like NFTE so schooling can deliberately cultivate the virtues of a flourishing entrepreneurial life.

book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know
samples: The editors' introduction argues that Dracula's century-long grip on popular culture says more about us than about the Count, asking why we willingly seek out an evening of nightmares in Stoker's novel and its movie spin-offs when, as Van Helsing's failures show, Dracula just cannot be killed. It frames the volume's guiding questions: is Dracula truly evil, is his taste for human blood really worse than our meat-eating, and what does our fascination with this outdated, oddly accented aristocrat expose hidden in our own subconscious?

Mahon argues that vampiric immortality is a curse not because it brings decrepitude (against Swift's Struldbruggs model, since Dracula and his brides keep eternal youth) but because intelligent vampires know endless boredom awaits: following Bernard Williams and Shelly Kagan, boredom replaces death as the inevitable evil, giving vampires a Heideggerian 'being-toward-undeath' and 'being-toward-endless-pain'. Dracula's risky move from castle, brides, and slaves in Transylvania to London is read as the boredom escape it is, and since vampires still resist destruction, Mahon weighs the tedium curse against the alternative curse of compelled psychopathic bloodlust, concluding that staking Dracula is involuntary euthanasia - a mercy killing.

Pramik maps Kierkegaard's three stages from Either/Or and Stages on Life's Way onto the novel: Dracula lives the aesthetic stage of pleasure and possessive power (imprisoning Harker in the castle, refusing to let the brides feed on him), Harker the anxious ethical stage of moral rules and guilt, and Van Helsing the religious stage of faith 'by virtue of the absurd' - trusting God to do the impossible through crucifixes, garlic, and the beheading of Lucy. Against Seward's doubting questions about these absurd tactics, she argues that Van Helsing's renewed, tested faith proves itself and makes him the book's real hero, since neither pleasure nor ethics alone defeats Dracula or gives life meaning.

Willis and Strunk read the scene where Dracula forces Mina to drink blood from his bare chest through Plotinus's Enneads: the mutual blood exchange is a dark unicity, a perverted oneness joining life and death, through which the soulless, blood-dependent Count tries to steal Mina's agency, Intellect, and her link to the world soul because he cannot be self-sufficient or create his own meaning. Their interconnected minds are also his undoing - Mina's hypnotic bond tracks Dracula to his coffin, and his destruction at Van Helsing's hands frees her - so the chapter concludes that this perversion of Plotinian oneness exposes our fear that the veil between the living and the dead is dangerously thin.

Jordan asks what makes Dracula obey his rules (no entry without an invitation, native soil, garlic, the crucifix) when he obeys no morality: self-imposed Kantian moral rules and a vampire-cabal enforcing Hohfeldian duties both fail because the Count's self-interest is too strong, so the rules must be natural law set by God or nature. He then uses Wesley Hohfeld's jural relations (duty, claim, liberty, power, immunity, liability, disability) to analyze Dracula's rule over his brides, servants, and victims - Lucy's lost consent shifting power and letting the Count through her door - concluding that only this legal-relations analysis plus natural law explains both Dracula's restraints and his apparent violations of physics like defying gravity and commanding the weather.

Arp starts from Dracula's inability to love or find satisfaction and his awareness of it, then deploys Sidgwick's hedonistic paradox: pursuing pleasure for its own sake yields pain whether or not the pleasure is found, through mistaking pain for pleasure (Lestat on the dead twins), boredom, or emptiness. Mill's distinction between lower bodily and higher mental pleasures explains how vampires can enjoy the bodily pleasure of blood yet lament lacking joy and love, while substance versus property dualism (Plato as the substance dualist) frames whether the Count's soul survives when his body crumbles to dust. Aristotle's Book X pleasures of completed states and the 'virtuous vampires' from Barnabas Collins to St. Germain show the only escape from the dilemma: pursue activities for their own sake and higher mental pleasures rather than bodily pleasure alone.

book: 091 - It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed
samples: Using 'Flowers for Charlie', where a placebo pill convinces two scientists and even the Waitress that Charlie has become a genius, the chapter asks what actually makes something philosophy. Sounding smart is not philosophy: big words, the Sokal-style hoax paper submitted to a leading journal, and the 'Guru Effect' of credulous admirers all fail, yet Charlie's pronouncements turn out true by sheer luck - which is exactly Edmund Gettier's problem of epistemic luck illustrated with the broken-clock example. Since we can never verify our premises or our reasoning, the chapter sides with Aristotle's response to Plato's theory of forms that we can never determine what a thing is, only what it is not, and concludes the show is philosophical precisely because the Gang is the exact antithesis of reality, truth, and right action.

Greg Littmann systematically compares the Gang's values - wealth, attention, bad-assery ('Project Badass'), sexual conquest, relentless competition, revenge, pride in cheating, and callousness toward even friends and family - with the values Homer's Iliad and Odyssey celebrate, showing Achilles and Odysseus behave like the Gang: sacking cities, taking women as war trophies like Briseis, boasting of deception (the Trojan Horse), and rigging the funeral games. The real difference is scope: the heroes honor bonds of loyalty to comrades, family, and their own communities where the Gang is loyal to no one, and moderns extend concern further still. Yet our morals fail the same way when people are far enough removed - we tolerate homelessness, prison rape, sweatshop goods, and national glory-seeking - so the chapter pleads for the universal moral principles Greek moral philosophy first sought against Homeric values.

Jason Iuliano reads the Gang's 'no restrictions' motto as egoistic hedonism in the tradition of Aristippus of Cyrene: pleasure alone is intrinsically good, and specifically present, bodily, personal pleasure - exactly how Mac defends his fifty-pound weight gain and the pair's decision to smoke crack. The doctrine is shown in action through the Gang's treatment of Rickety Cricket, used as a mere instrument while his life is ruined without a flicker of guilt, and through get-rich-quick schemes from the impulse-bought boat to running for comptroller purely for the bribe. Robert Nozick's Experience Machine then shows why hedonism fails - we want to actually do things, be a certain kind of person, and touch reality, not float as an 'indeterminate blob' - and Mill's paradox of hedonism explains the Gang's misery: pursuing pleasure directly is precisely what drives it away.

Christopher Ketcham's mock lost episode 'Charlie Gets Beatified' - in which Frank fakes a water-into-wine miracle with red food dye so the Gang can monetize Charlie's canonization - frames a genuine exercise in medieval modal metaphysics. Aristotle's definition of contingency, on which opposites can occur only at different times, is set against Duns Scotus's view that something can be otherwise at the very moment it acts, so that God's immutable foreknowledge coexists with a will 'endowed with something of his own freedom'. The chapter spells out necessity, contingency, and impossibility in possible-worlds terms (a gang needs at least two members in every world; Frank is impossible in Season One) and reads 'Gun Fever Too: Still Hot' as empirical confirmation of Scotus and Olivi: the Gang holds opposite positions within a single episode, proving real contingency and free will.

Charlene Elsby asks what makes the McPoyles cross the line from offensive (like the Gang) into irredeemably creepy, working through their bathrobes, unibrows, incest, and constant milk drinking. Her answer runs through violated social convention: the creepy person is not merely making non-standard choices but seems unaware conventions exist at all, and Liam's 'It's society that has the problem' raises moral relativism only for the chapter to insist the creep reaction tracks something actually wrong, not just different. Adding the legacy of physiognomy (we judge character from appearance, and more harshly when the trait is controllable) and an inductive inference (everything the McPoyles do is creepy, so even the milk must be), creepiness emerges as an art of detection rather than a science: whether someone is creepy differs from whether they seem creepy.

Daniel Leonard takes CharDee MacDennis, the Gang's three-level drinking game, as an unconscious confession read through Freud's structural model. The 'Mind' level - grudge trivia like 'Denis is asshole. Why Charlie hate?' and drawing-guessing 'based solely on feel' - runs on the id and the pleasure principle; the 'Body' level of darts, kennels, and the no-cursing rule is restraint, properly the ego's job of deferring gratification (which only Dennis's manipulative D.E.N.N.I.S. System grotesquely exercises); and the 'Spirit' level of Emotional Battery and Public Humiliation externalizes the superego's guilt and ego-ideal, with Frank as the all-seeing punishing father. The Gang's psychology is backwards - their 'Mind' level tests exactly what is not conscious - and their over-strong superegos surface in rationalization and the Black Card's coin flip, while smashing the losers' idealized game pieces enacts a wishful symbolic patricide.

samples: The volume's introduction, 'Learning from the Insiders.' It introduces Orange Is the New Black (Piper Kerman's book and the Netflix series about Piper's time in Litchfield) and previews each contributor's topic: other minds, manipulation, the Prisoner's Dilemma, religion, existentialism, race, Crazy Eyes as Don Quixote, prisoners' moral obligations, Nietzsche on a trans woman, Aristotle on friendship, Bentham's panopticon, and Foucault on punishment. It frames the show as ripe for philosophy on punishment, moral obligation, existential themes, and race, gender, identity, and sexuality without itself applying any single theory.

Hoyt argues the show's core lesson is dropping the little lies we tell ourselves: Bennett calls his crush on Daya 'love' to excuse framing Mendez, Pornstache is a man performing a blustering guard (Sartrean bad faith), and Larry and Polly's 'love just happened' dodges responsibility for betrayal. Piper's arc (the Colt 45 scene in '40 Oz. of Furlough') shows the payoff of authenticity, while Healy's Safe Place is a fantasy that cannot will a change of worldview. Using Wittgenstein's aspect-seeing from Philosophical Investigations, he shows how characters and viewers miss ethically significant meanings, like Taystee's shower 'compliment' as intimidation and Piper's convenient blindness to Soso's humanity when selling her for a blanket.

Robison-Greene asks whether there are principled standards for 'shipping' TV couples and applies Platonic-Aristotelian flourishing criteria (long-term safety, emotional needs, trust, and mutual growth toward virtue) to Piper's options: Alex fails on safety and trust (selling Piper out, the perjury advice), Larry fails on empathy and growth, so by real-life standards we should ship none of them. She concludes shipping is mostly aesthetic, then proposes minimal moral rules for our attitudes toward fictional relationships: never ship Pornstache, respect consent, and never let race, gender, or orientation decide.

DiEdoardo, a trans criminal-defense lawyer, reads Sophia Burset through Nietzsche: her 'why of life' (bringing her body into line with her gender identity) lets her endure the 'how' of misgendering by Figueroa, Red, and her wife Crystal, plus a sentencing disparity she compares to Piper's lighter drug deal. Burset's rational appeals ('Lesbian Request Denied,' her WAC run) fail, confirming Nietzsche's disdain for dialectics, but in 'A Whole Other Hole' she stops asking and acts, teaching the inmates vulval anatomy until Taystee's 'she's right' marks her acceptance. She is the 'creator' who breaks the tables of values, migrating from freak to woman with unique knowledge.

Carveth examines African-American portrayal on the show through Piper, Taystee, and Sophia: Piper's whiteness wins Healy's favoritism and makes her complicit in keeping the inmates powerless ('we understand each other, don't we?'), while Taystee's parole violation shows Litchfield as the only place she fits. Using Lippmann's account of media stereotypes, he credits the show with multidimensional characters of color but faults it for a 'white voice': Black women's incarceration is framed as bad choices and culture of poverty, and only Piper's SHU suffering is shown while Black and Latina women cycle through it. The series critiques the prison system yet stops short of showing the structural forces that leave its inmates no options.

Ketcham greets Piper Kerman at the prison door with Bentham's ghost: the state's utility calculation of her drug money laundering, the rat's discounted sentence, and the design of the panopticon, whose one-way inspection tower was meant to make surveillance cheap, obedience automatic, and prisoners productive and even saved. He contrasts that reform vision with the reality reconstructed from the book, where punishment falls on everyone, including families paying commissary prices and denied visits, and Danbury's 'vocational training' amounts to changing light bulbs. Bentham's own principle that 'punishment is an evil' is turned against a system that warehouses rather than rehabilitates.

samples: The editors' introduction: it surveys what changed since the first Doctor Who and Philosophy volume (the War Doctor, the Trenzalore death and survival, the Impossible Girl, Dalek divine hatred, the Master becoming 'the Mistress') and previews the volume's questions—whether Clara is possible, whether the Doctor may lie, whether he could have avoided Trenzalore, and whether the Ninth Doctor's 'coward, any day' pacifism gave way to the Twelfth's less-pacifistic cowboy streak. It also introduces the fandom insiders (podcasters, convention runners, a Time Lord Rock musician) who serve as 'Time Lord Presiding' over each Serial, framing the book around the show's emphasis on personal identity and time paradoxes.

Siler answers the Twelfth Doctor's question 'Am I a good man?' from 'Into the Dalek' by arguing that goodness is the Doctor's 'magnetic north'—the stable moral orientation his regenerations bend back toward, the force that drove him from Gallifrey's corrupt Time Lords. He concedes a dark side, from the would-be caveman killing of 'An Unearthly Child' to the 'Time Lord Victorious' arrogance of 'The Waters of Mars,' but insists character must be judged over a whole life, including the Doctor's effect on companions like Jo Grant, Leela, Ace, and Rose, whom he teaches 'a better way of livin' your life.' Clara's closing verdict—that he tries to be good and 'that's probably the point'—caps the claim that a settled direction of character, not perfection, makes him a good man.

Pless argues the Doctor's shift from the Ninth's self-avowed 'coward, any day' to the Eleventh's gun-toting action hero tracks real-world politics and markets rather than internal story logic: after the 7/7 London bombings and amid the War on Terror, and as the show's global export grew, a war-weary British ideal gave way to the decisive 'Oncoming Storm.' She traces the arc through the Tenth's gleeful xenocide of the Racnoss in 'The Runaway Bride,' the eternal punishment of the Family of Blood, the Eleventh brainwashing humanity to exterminate the Silence in 'Day of the Moon,' and the assault of 'A Good Man Goes to War,' before 'The Day of the Doctor' retcons the Time War so the Doctor never destroyed the Time Lords, validating the action-hero persona. Her conclusion: in a crisis culture demanding proactive heroes, cowardice—once the Doctor's honest self-assessment—was rebranded as vice.

Dray reads Doctor Who as a metaphor for television itself: the Doctor and his box emerge from a junkyard just after FCC chairman Newton Minow called TV a 'vast wasteland,' and the show turns the medium's supposed weaknesses—shaky effects, departing actors, budget limits—into its fiction, most famously converting William Hartnell's failing health into regeneration. Following 'An Unearthly Child' through the cancellation-era New Adventures novels, the flawed 1996 TV movie, and the Davies and Moffat eras (including Amy literally believing the erased Doctor back into existence in 'The Big Bang'), he argues television's iterative, audience-entangled, endlessly rewritable nature is the show's real subject. The TARDIS, 'bigger on the inside,' is television itself, and 'The Day of the Doctor' celebrates a medium that can remake the old anew—self-interrogating its own dangers in stories like 'The Idiot's Lantern' and 'Bad Wolf.'

Sas uses literary alchemy's three-stage magnum opus to read 'Midnight' as the nigredo—the black stage of dissolution that begins the Tenth Doctor's arc of purification, death, and rebirth ending in his regeneration in 'The End of Time.' She shows Russell T Davies loading the episode with nigredo imagery: the deadly Xtonic sunlight that calcinates bodies to ash, the planet of endless 'midnight' and witching-hour folklore, the Salem-style mob panic modeled on The Crucible as the mimicking Sky drives the passengers to demand a sacrificial victim, and the Doctor stripped of TARDIS, companion Donna, authority, and finally his voice. The Doctor's humbling—he solves nothing and is saved only by the Hostess's self-sacrifice—purges the ego that later swells into 'Time Lord Victorious,' while his reunion with the fiery Donna foreshadows the alchemical fusion of the DoctorDonna and eventual rebirth.

Smith asks how one Clara can exist as Oswin the converted Dalek, a Victorian governess, and a present-day nanny, and answers with philosophy of mind: after the real Clara steps into the Doctor's timeline on Trenzalore, the 'echoes' are best understood as manifestations within the Doctor's own subconscious, read through Freud's dream interpretation and id-ego-superego (the echoes act as his conscience) and Jung's archetypes, collective unconscious, individuation, and synchronicity—her name meaning clarity, her red wardrobe marking the copies, and the leaf of 'The Rings of Akhaten' as the meaningful coincidence that produced her. Aristotle's Categories frames what Oswin still shares with humanity after Dalek conversion, and the soufflé-is-the-recipe line together with social-cognition research on multiple selves supports the conclusion that the Claras are metaphysically the same person despite different bodies and roles—making the 'Impossible Girl' possible.

samples: The editor's introduction argues that Roth's series does not just contain philosophy but actually does it, proposing hypotheses about virtue, social order, evil, and forgiveness and testing them for consistency. It casts Tris as a Socratic figure who retraces the Allegory of the Cave: she starts 'chained' inside the cave of Chicago's faction system, climbs out to discover the faction life is a lie, and is tortured and eventually killed for the truth she tries to bring back, just as the cave-dwellers would kill the returning prisoner. The introduction closes by insisting the series is really about choice - that wisdom, unlike knowledge, must be lived, that self-reflection and even self-doubt are the hallmark of the wise, and that when life offers no options, like Tris and the factionless, you have to create your own.

Seymour argues that the serums of Roth's world mirror the real-world medical control of young people: with no objective test, about 6.4 million American children are diagnosed with ADHD and medicated for diverging from adult-defined 'normal' behavior, just as Amity bakes peace serum into its bread and Dauntless uses simulation and truth serums on initiates. Tris's Divergence, and especially her failure to resist the peace serum because some part of her wanted to stop feeling, shows that the desire to conform is what makes chemical control work, while Tobias (re-running his own fear landscape) and Peter (erasing his own memory) model appropriating the serums as tools of self-control. Tris's resistance to the Bureau's memory serum then becomes a vicarious experience of power for young readers who face medication for their own 'divergence.'

Ketcham reads the faction system as the Bureau's behavioral-correction experiment after a eugenics disaster, and compares the Bureau to the Tuskegee syphilis study: subjects who never gave informed consent, were denied treatment, and were treated as expendable because 'the experiment must continue at all costs.' He maps W.E.B. Du Bois's 'twoness' - double consciousness - onto Tris, who thrives in Dauntless yet belongs to no faction, and onto Tobias, whose identity collapses when he learns he tests as merely Dauntless. Closing with Gramsci, he argues Chicagoans have bought into the oppressor's story about genes and factions, so they need an organic intellectual to lead them out of the cave, and proposes Freire's praxis as the unfinished sequel.

Rhine argues that Tris's heroism rests on Buddhist practice: her breath-counting on the Ferris wheel and inside Four's fear landscape, her emotional intelligence, and her awareness of the parental 'voices in her head' are classic meditative disciplines for calming the ego whose clinging, on the Buddhist account, is the cause of suffering (dukkha). She reads Abnegation's gray houses, plain food, and four-times-a-year mirror as ritual ego-diminishment - a middle way between indulgence and the extreme asceticism the Buddha rejected - that explains why most Divergent arise from Abnegation. Contemporary neuroscience is then recruited: the amygdala-versus-prefrontal-cortex struggle Will describes, and monks' heightened gamma waves, explain how Tris can see the simulation as a simulation, like Neo in The Matrix, and act while others are paralyzed by fear.

Mallalieu uses Nietzsche's slave morality, will to power, and Ubermensch to read Roth's social experiment: Abnegation's foot-washing, guilt-driven selflessness is slave morality, Amity's drugged peace makes them willing slaves, and Peter - cruel, self-promoting, guilt-ridden - is the most Nietzschean character, whose memory wipe is an attempt to forget his way out of slave morality. Even the heroes turn out Nietzschean when Tris and Tobias dose the Bureau with memory serum, since Nietzsche holds that the old values must be forgotten before new ones can be created. But the chapter concludes the price is too high: losing your values along with your memories means losing your identity ('I would rather be dead than empty'), so Nietzsche's imagined experiment, played out through the Bureau's tools, would be a world good only for the strong and cruel.

Bogosian argues the film locates evil not in human nature itself, as Jeanine claims when she calls human nature 'the enemy,' but in cultivable vices - Al's jealousy and fear of failure leading to attempted murder and suicide, Eric's and Jeanine's lust for power - and that only altruistic, self-sacrificial love can counteract them. With Aristotle's point that friendship is essential to developing virtue and to the good life, he shows the faction system fails on its own terms: a single virtue in isolation corrupts (Candor's truth without kindness), and a system that removes real moral and political freedom destroys the flourishing it promises. Tris's parents' sacrifices and the Tris-Four relationship - honest training advice, protection of her Divergence, and the gun-to-her-own-forehead scene where love breaks the simulation's grip - model the love that overcomes the corrupt system.
